sentence: This is a 22-year-old male, asthenic, weak and thin, who comes to our health center consultation repeatedly in the last month, due to stabbing epigastric pain associated with postprandial nausea and vomiting that relieves the pain.
The episodes have been occurring for 7 years, which is why he has consulted the emergency services on multiple occasions, without acute pathology ever being found.

He was admitted 3 years ago for one of these episodes, and a gastric biopsy with gastric biopsy was performed, which was positive for H. pylori; He completed eradication treatment with current triple therapy (omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin), with a subsequent negative breath test for H. pylori infection.
Due to persistence of symptoms, treatment with antiemetics and multiple proton pump inhibitors was initiated, with no long-term response.

Upon his admission, he was evaluated by the Mental Health service, since the symptoms of acute pain that subsided with vomiting persisted, and he was diagnosed with anxious-depressive syndrome with poor follow-up and therapeutic non-compliance.
He had no allergies to food or drugs.
Currently, the pain subsided in the genupectoral position and with cannabis consumption.
On examination we found a patient with stable vital signs, with a BMI of 17.7.
His abdomen is excavated, tympanic, soft and slightly painful on deep palpation in the epigastrium, with no masses, lymphadenopathy or megalia being palpable.

The analysis did not show any alterations; absence of anemia, negative inflammatory response markers, no liver alterations or electrolyte alterations, total proteins 5.8 g/dL (normal value of 6.4 to 8.3 g/dL).
On abdominal x-ray there are no signs of intestinal obstruction.

A total abdominal ultrasound was performed in our office in the supine position, with no evidence of relevant findings, so we decided to consult with the Digestive service, where, after being evaluated, a barium intestinal transit was requested, with a delay of more than 8 hours due to slow gastric emptying due to a permanent decrease in caliber in the 3rd duodenal portion, suggestive of extrinsic compression, which did not prevent the distal passage of contrast, all of which is compatible with vascular compression.
Given this finding, it was decided to perform an abdominal CT angiography, with the result of a vascular clamp that produced compression of the duodenum in its 3rd portion.
The mesenteric clamp affected the duodenum and the left renal vein, producing compression and dilation before and after compression.
